pillars.title: The three pillars
pillars.caption: The pillars are reciprocal rather than sequential. Regulation widens what a person can meet; a workable structure protects the time and recovery that regulation needs; participation turns both into lived experience and says what actually helps.

items.name: Nervous system regulation
items.question: Can I meet this experience with enough flexibility to respond?
items.body: Developing enough steadiness, flexibility, and responsiveness to stay in contact with what is happening, and still have some choice about how you meet it.

items.name: Minimal viable life
items.question: Does my life structure support basic needs, growth, and room to be?
items.body: The smallest arrangement of practical supports, obligations, and opportunities that lets a person function while keeping room for growth and enjoyment.
items.link: Read about the minimal viable life

items.name: Participation
items.question: How can I bring myself into the life available, without claiming every outcome?
items.body: Bringing your voice, values, and choices into your life through authorship, while releasing the claim to control what other people, circumstances, and chance will do.

zones.title: Green, Yellow, and Red
zones.caption: A teaching metaphor rather than a diagnostic scale. People experience these states differently, the boundaries between them are not sharp, and none of them is a moral category.

items.name: Green
items.body: Relative regulation — enough safety, openness, curiosity, connection, and choice to meet the moment without being driven entirely by urgency. Compatible with alertness, work, challenge, and focused effort; Green is not the same thing as being passive.

items.name: Yellow
items.body: Mobilisation and activation — heightened effort, anticipation, vigilance, pressure, excitement, or readiness. Chosen deliberately, Yellow is where meaningful work, learning, and intensity happen. It becomes a problem when it settles into an ambient condition with no recovery.

items.name: Red
items.body: Overwhelm, shutdown, defensive narrowing, or depletion: the loss of workable flexibility. It can look like agitation, avoidance, numbness, or an inability to start. Red is a signal about load and available capacity, not a verdict on character.

layers.title: The three layers of a viable life
layers.caption: Assessed across an ordinary week or season, not against a perfect day. A structure that is efficient but systematically excludes enjoyment and free attention has failed the test of viability, however productive it looks.

items.name: Foundation
items.body: Somatic, biological, and practical care: sleep, nourishment, movement, recovery, health needs, a manageable physical environment, and the essential tasks that keep a life running. Not a universal checklist — the question is what this person needs, given the resources and the responsibilities they actually have.

items.name: Maintenance and expansion
items.body: Maintenance keeps what already works: money, work, household, health, relationships, existing commitments. Expansion is deliberate growth: study, skills, new relationships, creative work, meaningful risk. Choose a small number of growth tracks and let the rest sit at a sustainable level.

items.name: Unstructured being
items.body: Play, pleasure, curiosity, friendship, creativity, rest, connection, spontaneity — the experiences that need no justification in terms of output. Not a reward for finishing the list, but part of the reason the list exists at all.
